The Black caracara (Daptrius ater) exhibits a pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with adult females attaining a substantially larger asymptotic mass than males. Field measurements from museum specimen series indicate that female ultimate wet weight reaches approximately 385 grams [Wwi = approximately 385 grams], whereas males are considerably lighter, with a documented maximum adult body mass of 330 grams [Wwi = 330 grams]. This difference in size is reflected across several life-history traits and likely influences competitive dynamics during foraging and nest defense. Under thermal conditions typical of actively brooded clutches (40 °C [T = 40 °C]), the incubation period for this species, based on observations of the closely related yellow-headed caracara (Daptrius chimachima), lasts for 22 days [ab = 22 days], a value that represents the typical core temperature of an actively brooded clutch. Upon hatching, the altricial nestling emerges at a relatively low initial wet weight of 53.9 grams [Ww0 = 53.9 grams], a figure derived from the proportional relationship between neonatal mass and adult female mass. This modest starting mass underscores the heavy parental investment required over the subsequent weeks.

Developmental milestones under captive conditions, standardized to the typical avian body temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], reveal a compact early life history for this raptorial species. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at 19 days after hatching [tx = 19 days after hatching], a timing estimated from the ontogenetic schedule documented in the congener Daptrius chimachima at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively early departure from the nest is characteristic of falconiform birds that rely on open, accessible habitats where prolonged brooding may increase predation risk. The downy chick develops pin feathers rapidly, and by the time of fledging, the juvenile bird is capable of short, controlled flights between perches. Following nest departure, the fledgling remains dependent on parental provisioning for a period, gradually refining its hunting skills through practice and observation. This brief nestling phase is a critical component of a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid development under consistently warm thermal conditions.

Puberty, or the onset of gonadal maturation, is attained relatively quickly in Black caracaras held under captive conditions at a body temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], with individuals reaching reproductive maturity at 54 days since birth [tp = 54 days since birth]. This value indicates that the species is capable of maturing within its first year, a trait that facilitates rapid population turnover in dynamic neotropical environments. In contrast, the actual initiation of breeding, or the time since birth at first brood, is considerably delayed; field observations indicate that first reproduction typically occurs at 803 days since birth [tR = 803 days since birth] under the same thermal regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This lag between physiological puberty and effective breeding is common among raptors that require an extended period of territory establishment, pair bonding, and the development of proficient foraging skills before undertaking the substantial energetic commitment of reproduction. The delay likely serves to maximize the probability of successful fledging from the first nesting attempt.

The maximum recorded longevity for wild Black caracaras, based on recapture data and monitored under the standard physiological temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], is 5475 days [am = 5475 days]. This lifespan is moderate for a raptor of its body size and suggests a life-history strategy balanced between the rapid maturation typical of small falconids and the extended senescence schedules observed in larger accipitrids. The reproductive output of the species is constrained by both clutch size and annual nesting frequency. Females lay 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per clutch], a typical range for birds of this family, and they produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. The combination of moderate fecundity per event with infrequent annual reproduction places a premium on high nestling survival and effective parental care to maintain stable population numbers.

Metabolic investigations conducted under controlled thermal conditions provide insight into the energetic demands of this species. The basal metabolic rate, measured as resting oxygen consumption in post-absorptive adults at an ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], reaches a maximum of 216 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 216 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This respiratory value reflects the high metabolic intensity required to sustain the active, predatory lifestyle of a tropical falconiform bird. When considering the substantial size dimorphism between sexes, the mass-specific metabolic rate is likely higher in males given their lower adult body mass. The elevated BMR recorded at this thermoneutral temperature also has implications for the species' foraging ecology, as it necessitates a consistently high prey intake rate. These energetic constraints, together with the comparatively fast developmental schedule for puberty and fledging, paint a picture of a species finely attuned to the productive, resource-rich environments of the Amazon and Orinoco basins where it is most commonly encountered.
